item.title: [ 30] Dark Souls 3 endings
item.description:
Which ending is the best?
I personally like End of Fire the most, because it feels like the most natural and fitting end to the First Flame. The fact that distant embers might one day reignite the flame is a hopeful counterpoint to the theme of entropy present since the first game. On a personal level, spending those final moments with the Fire Keeper isn't all that bad either.
I don't like usurpation all that much. It's visually cool, but the power fantasy of it feels anti Dark Souls. Yuria hot though.

item.title: [ 41] Elon Musk Melts Down Over Perfectly Normal Questions in Wild New Interview
item.description:
https://gizmodo.com/elon-musk-economist-interview-2000790016

Elon Musk sat down with the editor-in-chief of the Economist for a taped interview that went live Thursday. The Tesla CEO has been avoiding normal journalists recently, even cancelling a planned interview with CNBC earlier this month. And it now seems pretty obvious why. Musk has a hard time answering normal questions about his often fascist and sometimes incoherent worldview.

The interview started cordially enough, with Economist editor Zanny Minton Beddoes asking Musk about his thoughts on the future of artificial intelligence. Musk said many things that he’s said before, including that AI will deliver an age of abundance, where “anyone can have anything they think of.”

Musk insisted that AI will exceed human intelligence in five years and that humans will no longer be in charge of the world in 10 years. Beddoes pressed Musk several times on what that means and how his companies will continue to exist. The billionaire rambled on and on in a way that didn’t really stand up to any scrutiny.

“If you have vast numbers of robots with vast amounts of digital intelligence, you have a sort of a quasi-infinite economy,” said Musk. “The future is going to be very, very different from the past. There’s no analogy or metaphor that I think illustrates the magnitude of change that we’re going to experience here.”

item.title: [ 33] Why does America reward investors far more than it rewards workers? It's a w
item.description:
Why does America reward investors far more than it rewards workers?

It's a weird paradox because societies need lots of hard work in order to maintain themselves and all their system. Maintaining a system of laws and justice requires a lot of work. Maintaining a sewage system requires a lot of work. Maintaining ports and water ways requires a lot of work.

However, workers are the most abused and lowest paid group of Americans. In contrast, investors make money simply off owning things. You can literally buy stock and just do nothing but sit on your ass holding for 5 years and make a handsome profit.

The system we currently have does not incentivise work at all. Instead it incentives the lack of work because that yields the lowest reward.

item.title: [ 72] House advances bill barring sitting Congress members from buying stocks
item.description:
https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/22/house-congressional-stock-trading.html?msockid=196670d327c565552f78675826d66426

The U.S. House advanced legislation on Wednesday that would stop members of Congress from buying individual stocks while in office, taking the first meaningful action on an issue that has dogged lawmakers for years.

The bill passed on a vote of 232-198, with more than a dozen Democrats joining Republicans in support.

There is broad public support for a ban on members of Congress trading while in office, as lawmakers’ well-timed trades and booming portfolios have raised insider trading concerns among ethics watchdogs and drawn intense public scrutiny going back decades.

But the GOP-led legislation advanced by the House, dubbed the Stop Insider Trading Act, falls well short of what the most vocal advocates of a congressional trading ban have called for. And many Democrats had lined up against the proposal.

“I’m very disappointed in it. It’s a stock trading ban that still allows stock trading. It’s a weak bill,” Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., part of a bipartisan coalition that has advocated for a more thorough ban, told CNBC.

item.title: [ 42] AIPAC Is Losing Its Sway Over Democrats
item.description:
The pro-Israel group’s absolutist stance has alienated even moderate Democrats who support the Jewish state.

https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/aipac-losing-sway-over-democrats-111559774.html

WASHINGTON — In 2024, a super PAC allied with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent $4 million to boost then-state Sen. Sarah Elfreth in a contested Democratic primary in Maryland. It’s not an exaggeration to say the money was decisive: It was more than twice as much as Elfreth’s campaign raised and spent.

It was one of a string of wins for AIPAC in Democratic primaries, starting in 2022, when it backed candidates who would keep military aid flowing to Israel. The group has long been clear about what it expects from candidates it backs: There should be no conditions on aid to Israel under any circumstances.

But last week, Elfreth was one of the 10 Democrats who voted “present” on a symbolic amendment to cut off aid to Israel, signaling an unwillingness to shoot down the effort completely. Another 21 Democrats who had received financial backing from AIPAC voted for the amendment. Altogether, 103 Democrats voted for the amendment in a rebuke of Israel and its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has overseen a war in Gaza that has led to more than 70,000 deaths.

In a lengthy statement, Elfreth called the vote a ploy by House Republican leaders to divide Democrats. She said the amendment was poorly written, but also, regarding Israel, that “the current dynamics of our allyship are not sustainable for the region and our nation.”

AIPAC appeared to cut off fundraising support to the Democrats who voted yes. One of them, Rep. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.), said he welcomed the consequences.
